parts: Family income is the money, goods and services available to the family to fulfil its needs and desires: money income (salary, business, rent, interest, household production sold) plus real income (goods and services enjoyed: free house or car from the employer, kitchen garden produce, doing chores or stitching clothes yourself, caring for equipment). Family income = money income + real income. Needs (basic: food, clothing and shelter; secondary: transport, education, entertainment) must be met first; then desires: comforts (cooler, fan) and luxuries (air-conditioner).

Expenditure is the money spent on goods and services. A spending plan divides money income among food, clothing, housing, education, transport, services, entertainment and savings; primary needs come first, then secondary needs, then desires (comforts before luxuries); each area must last the full month; keep expenditure less than income to save. Income management is the planned and controlled use of family income: planning (including savings) and controlling (avoid waste, buy from cooperative stores or wholesale markets, use time, energy and skill to cut costs: real income). There is no ready-made plan, because families with the same income have different needs.

A record has date, income, item purchased, quantity, rate, amount spent and balance (balance = previous balance − the day's expenses; e.g. Rs 5,000 − 478 = Rs 4,522). Advantages: shows exactly how much is spent and on what, checks unnecessary spending, compares months, helps plan the future and shows market trends.

Income generating activities (pickles, jams, stitching, knitting, toys, tuition), part-time jobs, investing savings to earn interest, wise use of resources (renting part of a house, lending a tractor) and cutting expenditure (doing cleaning or ironing yourself): 'money saved is money earned'.

Savings are the part of present income put aside for emergency or future use. Reasons: a secure future after retirement, emergencies (illness, accident), family goals (house, car), raising the standard of living (washing machine; or buy on instalments), and starting a small business. Guidelines: a realistic plan, a regular plan and a clear purpose. Investment means making savings grow (money kept at home does not grow, can be stolen and tempts spending). Financial institutions keep money safe, pay interest, allow withdrawal and give loans.

Avenues: Bank (safe, interest, withdrawal, loan against fixed deposit; savings account needs a form, signature, two photographs and an introducer; pass book, cheque book and nominee). Post office (convenient, start with Rs 20, tax-free interest in schemes like NSC and Indira Vikas Patra, rebate). Provident Fund (compulsory saving; GPF for salaried, PPF for the self-employed through the SBI or post office; interest and deposits exempt from tax; loan facility). Insurance (general insurance against theft, fire or flood, one-year contract; life insurance: premium, money with interest returned or paid to the nominee/beneficiary on death, tax relief, forced saving). UTI (units of face value Rs 10, minimum 100, dividends exempt from tax, can be encashed, safe). Shares (part ownership, share profit and loss, high return but risky, depends on the Sensex). Debentures or bonds (a loan to the company with fixed interest irrespective of profit; safer than shares). Property or jewellery (can pledge for loans but selling may take time or lose weight). Table of characteristics: savings bank account, post office savings account and units offer liquidity; NSC, GPF, PPF, life insurance and units give tax benefits; GPF, PPF and life insurance offer loan facility.

Selecting an investment: capacity to save, safety, higher rate of interest, easy liquidity, other benefits (dividends, tax relief), purchasing power (return should exceed inflation) and convenient place. Other facilities: credit card (plastic money; high interest on outstanding balance), debit card (issued against a savings account and debited automatically), ATM card (24-hour cash), loans (personal, education, house and vehicle; against a guarantee, bond or security) and e-banking (balance, bills, tickets, payments through the internet).
